messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Trouble with multivariate probit
parts:
I am having trouble getting running a very simple multivariate probit model in Stan. It has no predictors, just the intercept. Essentially, you have

    for (i in 1:N)
        y[i] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);

with the observed data z[i] being a vector of 0's and 1's, with z[i,k] = 1 if y[i,k] > 0 and z[i,k] = 0 if y[i,k] < 0. I have attached two different implementations I have tried: mvprobit1.stan is the most straightforward, and mvprobit.stan is an attempted optimization of the model.

I have tested both implementations using chains = 4, iter = 4000, with synthetic data generated as follows:

    K <- 5
    N <- 10000
    mu <- c(-0.3, +0.6, -1.5, +1.7, 0.0)
    rho <- 0.4
    Sigma <- (1 - rho) * diag(K) + matrix(rho, nrow = K, ncol = K)  # unit variances, correlations of 0.4
    Z <- t(MASS::mvrnorm(N, mu, Sigma) > 0) + 0
    data <- list(
      K = K,
      N = N,
      z = Z,
      eta = 1,
      sigma_mu = 5
    )

The straightforward implementation (mvprobit1.stan) performs miserably: lp__ has an Rhat of 2.11 and n_eff of 3. The optimized implementation performs somewhat better, but still very badly -- if I remember correctly, Rhat is 1.4 or thereabouts, and n_eff is around 17 for lp__.

Any thoughts on why this model is so troublesome for Stan, and what I can do to make it run better?

messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Re: Trouble with multivariate probit
parts:
Thanks for the pointer. I tried Bob's multivariate probit, but its performance is also very bad. I ran it twice with data generated the same way I described earlier, then reran my own mvprobit.stan and mvprobit1.stan again twice. In all cases I used 4 chains with 4000 iterations (2000 warmup, 2000 sampling) each. Here are the results I got for lp__ in all cases:

Bob's model:
  1. Rhat 1.06, n_eff 67
  2. Rhat 1.33, n_eff 21

mvprobit1.stan:

  1. Rhat 1.13, n_eff 22
  2. Rhat 1.23, n_eff  5
mvprobit.stan:

  1. Rhat 1.02, n_eff 201
  2. Rhat 1.07, n_eff 38

I remain puzzled as to why multivariate probit appears to be so difficult for Stan, and what, if anything, I can do to get better performance.

-- Kevin

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Trouble with multivariate probit
parts:
On Saturday, November 28, 2015 at 8:48:15 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
I remain puzzled as to why multivariate probit appears to be so difficult for Stan, and what, if anything, I can do to get better performance.

The dependence between the latent variables and the common parameters. I wouldn't focus too much on lp__ because its tails are very heavy in this case, but the overall performance is poor by Stan standards, even though the divergent transitions can be eliminated with a sufficiently high adapt_delta. Take a look at

pairs(stanfit, pars = c("L", "lp__"), las = 1)

for your data and you may see (even after disregarding the fixed margins) some nasty curves. I think you just have to run enough chains / iterations to get a decent n_eff.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Trouble with multivariate probit
parts:
On Tuesday, December 1, 2015 at 12:07:03 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I don't know multinomial probit --- is there not an equivalent for
softmax to normalize the probabilities?

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinomial_probit

Multinomial probit and multinomial logit (basically a softmax thing) are fundamentally different in that the former does not assume that the errors are uncorrelated / independent across outcome categories. Doing MCMC for a multinomial probit model is very difficult with either a Gibbs sampler or Stan.

Ben

messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Trouble with multivariate probit
parts:
Multivariate probit is fundamental to the application in question, because you really are interested in the underlying latent variables -- or at least their joint distribution. This kind of thing shows up a lot in marketing research where you have latent variables interpreted as an individual's utility for some product or choice option, and all you can actually observe are their choices, which in this application tells you whether the latent variable was greater than a threshold, and in other applications tells you which of several latent variables has the greatest value.

Note that the problem in this instance is not that the individual MCMC iterations are slow -- it's that the chain is mixing slowly, much more slowly than I am used to seeing with Stan, and this is with only a five-dimensional multivariate normal distribution on the latent vectors.

messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Trouble with multivariate probit
parts:
Multinomial probit and multivariate probit both involve computing rectangular probabilities

    Pr(a[1] <= x[1] <= b[1] and ... and a[n] <= x[n] <= b[n])

for multivariate normal distributions, and this is computationally difficult for any n beyond 2, or maybe 3. The GHK algorithm is sometimes used here, but it is a low-accuracy Monte Carlo algorithm, and when you try to use it within MCMC you generally get a smeared-out and distorted posterior. This, and the fact that the latent variables generally have a meaningful interpretation, is why augmenting with latent variables is often used in such models.
